The road ahead

Open Motion itself is still evolving quickly: it is developed as a web-based engine first, because that makes experimenting, trying new features and changing the editor system faster.

You are already running the native build: the editor runs on your device, works offline, and exports straight to your gallery or the share sheet.

What is the Open Motion engine?

Opus is a video timeline composition framework built on Kotlin Multiplatform, being developed by The Prismatic Company, which also involves developers who previously worked on Alight Motion.

Put simply, Opus provides the foundation for building apps that deal with video and motion graphics. The framework is designed to handle video, audio, images, text, compositing, animation, visual effects, multimedia timelines, preview, rendering, export, and other media needs.

It works in a way similar to Jetpack Compose / Compose Multiplatform, so timelines and media elements can react to state changes in real time while the user is editing.

Opus also already shows support for 3D space such as X, Y, Z positions, cameras, parallax and three-dimensional rotation, plus low-level APIs for GPU rendering and custom GLSL shaders.

Why is Open Motion interested in Opus?

Because Open Motion is not meant to become just an ordinary video editor. Open Motion is planned to grow into a motion graphics, animation, compositing and 3D editor.

Opus could become the multimedia engine foundation of Open Motion and handle timelines, video/audio decoding, playback, compositing, animation, effects, filters, GPU rendering, video export, and the 3D and camera systems.

If Opus turns out to be a good fit later, Open Motion would not have to build an entire multimedia engine from scratch. Development could focus on the parts that truly shape Open Motion's identity: the editor UI, keyframes, the timeline, animation workflow, tools, effects and other creative features.

Opus is built on Kotlin Multiplatform and is designed for use across several platforms. In its developer material, iPhone, iPad and macOS are already supported, while Android and Windows are still in development. Web and backend support are also planned.

Opus is also planned to become open source, but it is still being prepared before a public release.

Not a final decision

Opus is not certain to become Open Motion's final engine. Once the framework is actually released, it will be possible to see whether its performance, features, compatibility, licensing and development direction suit Open Motion's needs.

For now, Open Motion will keep growing as an experimental project while continuing to build features and try out new ideas.

Strong: every frame must enter the cache before the timeline advances. Uncached areas may slow down and go silent so audio does not drift; when the playhead returns to a ready cached area, audio plays in sync automatically.
Semi Strong: every missing frame gets a short window for an exact seek + capture. Playback may slow slightly and audio may pause briefly, but a single heavy frame cannot stall playback indefinitely.

Realtime Catch-Up: the playhead and audio stay real-time. B-frame-safe pre-render runs as a sequential cursor behind the playhead; on a slow device the green line falls behind instead of jumping ahead and leaving gaps. The worker keeps catching up to the part of the timeline already passed.

Normal: playback and audio stay real-time, but frames entering pre-render are decoded through the same sequential presentation-order pipeline as Strong/Record so B-frame video is safe. If the decoder cannot keep up, cached frames may be skipped without slowing playback.
Classic: every cached frame stays a raw ImageBitmap. Lightest on CPU, but far heavier on RAM and old frames are evicted once the limit is reached.

Video HW: frames near the playhead stay ImageBitmap, distant frames are compressed as WebCodecs video keyframes with a hardware preference. RAM and CPU use are usually far lower than PNG; preview quality is very high but not pixel-identical. Export stays native. ⚠️ Compatibility depends on the browser, the SoC and the codec driver. prefer-hardware is only a preference and does not guarantee that a hardware encoder is used; if the encoder/decoder is unsupported or fails, EditorsHub falls back to the Classic Cache automatically.
Lossless: frames near the playhead stay ImageBitmap, distant frames are compressed as lossless PNG. Cached FPS/pixel quality stays the same, using less RAM at the cost of extra CPU.
